case: Brunete drew Spanish, Italian and German fighters into the battle
mission: Four Republican I-16 and two I-15 squadrons faced three Nationalist-side Fiat squadrons at the opening. The later arrival of Grupo Morato and German 2./J 88 belongs to a separate stage.
observed_effect: Italian correspondence records Kindelán’s commendation of Italian fighters in the opening days and further requests for air support. This establishes that ground and air commands valued their intervention during the battle.
evidence_limit: Salas gives three opposing Fiat squadrons at the opening. The Italian unit chronology puts Nos. 19 and 20 at Torrijos-Barcience and treats No. 18 as a later arrival. A time-stamped field return is needed to place the third squadron on the first night and to identify all six Republican units.
source: Jesús Salas Larrazábal, Batalla de Brunete, Aeroplano 29
locator: p. 183, initial fighter force and reinforcements

case: Tremp escort and the loss of the Natachas
mission: Grupo 21’s 6ª and 7ª Escuadrillas took off at 14:45 with ten and nine fighters respectively to cover nine Natachas of Grupo 30’s 2ª Escuadrilla on the Llimiana mission.

evidence_limit: The Nationalist account records attacks, including one broken off without a visible result. Neither side supplies a reliable individual attacker for every missing bomber.

case: Warsaw’s defenders dispersed one formation while bombs reached Jabłonna
mission: The Pursuit Brigade scrambled III/1 and IV/1 Dywizjony. Its four organic escadrilles and attached 123rd are distinct from the 152nd, which assisted later. German 5. and 6.(K)/LG 1 met fighters while 4.(K)/LG 1 bombed Ciechanów.
observed_effect: By 16:00 Pawlikowski reported that one formation scattered on seeing III/1 while IV/1 saw three aircraft drop bombs on Jabłonna. The different observations explain why the same day contains both a local disruption and a completed bombing.
evidence_limit: The 16:00 Polish return lists one missing, one heavily damaged, one moderately damaged and eleven lightly damaged aircraft. A full-day loss return is still needed. Visual sightings do not identify the fate of each German bomber.
source: Col. Stefan Pawlikowski, Pursuit Brigade report to the Commander-in-Chief
source_type: facsimile and translation of wartime report
locator: PISM LOT.A.II.11/1d, document 2, pp. 104–105, 1 September 1939 at 16:00

case: Interception over Warsaw and damage at Okęcie
mission: Pilots of 111 and 112 Eskadry from Zielonka encountered the Bf 110s of I.(Z)/LG 1 covering III.(K)/LG 1. A separate air-warning message recorded damage at Okęcie.
observed_effect: The contemporary message distinguished the airframe works, which stopped operating, from the engine factory, which could continue. Contact by the Polish fighters and loss of production can both be traced on the day.
evidence_limit: The reporting chains locate the engagement and the damage in the same operational area. They do not identify which crew dropped the bomb that stopped the works.

case: Slovak fighters supported the southern front
mission: Two Slovak fighter detachments provided cover for German dive bombers from Kamenica nad Cirochou. Elements of 37. letka arrived on 9 September. Accounts disagree about which other unit arrived on 7 September.

case: Warsaw’s Pursuit Brigade withdrew to the Lublin area
mission: IPN follows the brigade through Zaborów and Radzików on 4–6 September, then to the Lublin area from 7 September. Its sorties could no longer be counted as fighters operating from the capital’s opening fields.

case: The Norwegian Army’s fighters met the invasion over Oslo
mission: Seven Gladiators of Jagervingen scrambled from Fornebu against incoming German aircraft. The Norwegian airframe history follows Gladiator 427 into combat with a Dornier Do 17.
observed_effect: Both machines force-landed, 427 near Kolsås and the Dornier near Bryn church. Its crew burned the German aircraft. Other Norwegian fighters landed at different locations as the defence broke up.
evidence_limit: The serial-level history establishes this pair of dispositions. The formation’s wider reported victories still require matching German loss returns.
source: Offisersbladet 2/2021, Fornebu and the Gladiators
locator: Jagervingen at Fornebu on 9 April, Gladiator 427 and Dornier at Bryn

case: Shore-based naval aircraft sank Königsberg in Bergen
mission: Skua dive bombers of 800 and 803 Naval Air Squadrons flew from Hatston against the German cruiser, which had remained in Bergen after gunfire damage the previous day.
observed_effect: The British naval diary recorded the attack. The independently written German Naval Staff diary placed the dive bombing at 08:00, described two bomb hits and fire, and recorded that the abandoned cruiser capsized at 11:00. The surviving crew joined the coastal defences.
evidence_limit: The German diary’s two reported hits belong to its own account. The ship’s later fate is firmer than any assignment of a specific hit to one British crew.
source: British Admiralty War Diary, April 1940
locator: Bergen, cruiser attack, 10 April entries

mission: Three 800 Squadron Skuas of Yellow Section took off from Ark Royal to protect shipping. They engaged He 111 1H+CT of 9./KG 26 as it bombed a British warship.

case: Land-based patrols during the recapture of Narvik
mission: RAF Nos. 263 and 46 Squadrons patrolled the battle area from Bardufoss. The Air Historical Branch counted 42 and 53 operational flights respectively and at most three aircraft airborne at once.
observed_effect: French troops entered Narvik and the Poles reached Beisfjord while the patrols continued. The forward base sustained cover during the assault. The campaign narrative then records the start of the already ordered evacuation.
evidence_limit: The reconstructed squadron record says Williams broke off short of fuel after observing smoke from a He 111 attacking a cruiser. Milligan’s evening attack had no visible result. Neither entry establishes a German write-off or that the whole assault depended on the patrols.
source: RAF Air Historical Branch, Campaign in Norway
locator: Narrative, p. 89, Narvik battle and 28 May operational flights

case: Dutch fighters flew from two fields before regrouping
mission: The 1e JaVA fought from De Kooy. At Schiphol nine Fokker D.XXIs of 2e JaVA took off during the attack. Some returned for fuel and flew again.

evidence_limit: The change of airfield explains how further flights remained possible. It does not reveal the number of serviceable machines available after every sortie.

case: Three Belgian escorts met German fighters over Vroenhoven
mission: Three Gladiators from the first platoon of Belgian 1/I/2 flew cover for Fairey Battles assigned to the bridges. Fighters of I./JG 1 intercepted them.

case: The RAF’s six Hurricane squadrons changed meaning in one day
mission: On 9 May the Air Component had four Hurricane squadrons. The AASF’s Nos. 1 and 73 bring the British total in France to six. Nos. 3 and 79 joined the Air Component on 10 May and No. 504 on 11 May.
observed_effect: The evening of 10 May therefore yields six in the Air Component alone. By 16 May Dowding described ten squadron-equivalents dispatched in recent days when arguing about the demands on home defence.
evidence_limit: The four squadron-equivalents ordered on 16 May came from eight different squadrons. Six flights crossed that day and two the next. Neither Dowding’s ten nor the order’s four should become a count of complete named units in France.
source: RAF Air Historical Branch, Campaign in France and the Low Countries
locator: Appendix L, Component Fighter Aircraft, scan p. 44, 9–17 May 1940

case: Fighter escorts reached London while RAF units fought and guarded their bases

case: Scramble orders, airborne reinforcements and a bomber at Victoria Station
mission: No. 11 Group ordered eleven squadrons up between 11:05 and 11:20. The five No. 12 Group squadrons airborne at 11:25 included Polish No. 302 and Czechoslovak No. 310. The museum also reproduces a combat report from a No. 72 pilot.

case: No. 129 Squadron at the Varengeville battery
mission: Twelve Spitfires of No. 129 Squadron supported No. 4 Commando's final assault on the six-gun coastal battery west of Dieppe. The Canadian Army history places the fighters' attack at 06:20.

case: Cover for the ships during the withdrawal
mission: No. 403 Squadron RCAF left at 11:15 and brought all twelve aircraft back at 13:15. Its 16:20 patrol saw the homeward convoy. On No. 411 Squadron's last patrol, its pilots attacked a Do 217 near the returning ships.

case: Smoke over the approaches at first light

case: What the Mustang crews could report inland
mission: Four army co-operation squadrons searched the roads for reinforcements. On No. 414 Squadron's first flight, Frederick Clarke and Hollis Hills were sent to check the Abbeville–Dieppe road. Hills recalled losing sight of his leader in darkness. Both returned to Gatwick.
observed_effect: Hills could see no traffic on the first flight. The RCAF history reports that the four squadrons' only positive sighting was of three to five supposed light tanks south of Dieppe. It concludes the identification was mistaken and that the Germans dealt with the landing from local resources.
evidence_limit: The four-squadron reconnaissance effort cost ten aircraft missing. The evidence does not attribute the tank report to No. 414 or establish that a commander changed a decision on receiving it.
source: Hollis Hills, recollection published by the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum
locator: Flightlines, March/April 2019, pp. 14–16, first patrol, Gatwick and return to Croydon.

case: Italian escorts shelter a torpedo attack on Pedestal
mission: The 2° and 22° Gruppi escorted the first torpedo formation. The 2° also covered the second. Of 43 torpedo bombers dispatched, 41 reached the convoy at about 13:00.

mission: No. 92 Squadron flew 42 sorties on 10 July covering the Pachino beaches from Malta. On 13 July eleven pilots patrolled en route to Pachino and landed there. On 14 July the squadron flew two patrols before its ground personnel arrived.

case: Ferry damage forced traffic away from the Salvatore jetty
mission: At 07:25 on 16 August eight No. 92 Squadron pilots covered 12 Warhawks attacking shipping. Six later escorted 12 Baltimores to Messina. A separate afternoon patrol covered warships southeast of Taormina.

case: What Romania’s fighter groups did before the pocket formed
mission: On 9 September the 6th Group sent eight aircraft on two sector-reconnaissance missions. The 7th logged 36 aircraft appearances on nine fighter sweeps, the 8th logged 19 on six familiarisation missions. evidence_limit: The 524 sorties span several roles. No paired German bomber loss series or Soviet interception return establishes how many losses the escort prevented. Parent-group totals do not prove every assigned squadron flew that day.

case: How many of the 26 Romanian squadrons can be named?
mission: The air force counted 26 in seven roles at the end of September. German mission correspondence gives group sizes and equipment. Comparison with a dated September squadron register identifies 17 by role, including the 108th medical unit.

case: The transports that reached Sixth Army
mission: On 29 November 38 Ju 52s and 21 He 111s took off. Twelve and thirteen, respectively, landed in the pocket. On 30 November the sources say 39 and 38 were committed, of which 30 and 36 landed.
observed_effect: The pocket received 25 aircraft landings from 59 take-offs on the 29th and 66 from 77 aircraft committed on the 30th. Richthofen’s diary separately records 75 tons delivered against a 300-ton order on 25 November.
evidence_limit: Commitment and take-off are different dispatch measures. An arrival is neither an aircraft loss nor a weighed cargo receipt. Daily manifests for 29–30 November and Sixth Army’s distribution below the airfield remain open.

case: Bobruisk: an aircrew’s bridge report alongside the ground encirclement
mission: On 27 June the 569th Assault Aviation Regiment attacked vehicles heading toward Titovka. Nine Pe-2s of the 24th Bomber Aviation Regiment were sent to the Berezina railway bridge at Bobruisk.

case: What the 16th Air Army could field and what actually flew
mission: The after-action report gives 3,037 serviceable aircraft before the offensive. The army records 2,531 aircraft flying 5,342 sorties on 16 April, including 1,188 day fighters on 2,545 sorties. Nineteen assigned regiments in three selected corps can be named.
observed_effect: The report attributes 6,548 sorties to the combined effort on this reporting front: 5,342 from 16th Air Army, 766 from 18th and 440 from 4th. The 17 April order names the 8th Guards Army’s sector as beneficiary of a further 6th Bomber Corps task.
evidence_limit: The compilation counts 3,033 combat aircraft out of 3,188 total. Its 114 reconnaissance and spotting aircraft differ from 51 plus 67 in the army return. Separately, the primary transcription’s first-day sortie categories sum to 5,352 (109 + 1,315 + 1,383 + 2,545), ten above its twice-stated 5,342. Neither discrepancy has been silently corrected.
source: Battle for Berlin, Soviet archive document edition
locator: Documents 136 and 143, 17 April ground-support order and 19 May after-action report, printed pp. 193–195 and 201–203; 16 April sortie and loss returns

case: Polish fighter cover along the northern advance
mission: Poland’s 1st Fighter Regiment left Mirosławiec for Barnówko on 14 April. It reported twelve flights on 16 April, when its responsibilities included cover for 1st Army’s crossing of the Oder. The regiment also identifies escort of Polish 3rd Assault Regiment near Bad Freienwalde.
observed_effect: The ground history records 1st Army establishing a bridgehead over the Oder, reaching the Alte Oder on 18 April and crossing it after further fighting on 19 April. This supplies a dated ground sequence in the same sector.
evidence_limit: The mapped Mirosławiec field was the departure base on 14 April. Barnówko was the operational base during the crossing; its surviving field description has not established a precise map point. The accounts do not isolate this escort’s effect on any individual crossing.
source: Krzemiński, Polish General Staff Academy study
locator: Berlin operation, pp. 38–39 and discussion of 1st Fighter Regiment, 4th Mixed Division and corps transfers 20–24 April

case: How many of the 18th Air Army’s Berlin sorties reached the target?
mission: The army’s overnight return lists 563 sorties for southwest Berlin. Of these, 517 aircraft reported bombing there: 139, 110, 201 and 60 from the four Guards Aviation Corps and seven from 45th Aviation Division.
observed_effect: Crews reported up to 30 fires and three large explosions. The first corps reported two Il-4s failing to return that night. The report also notes enemy fighter patrols and antiaircraft fire over Berlin.
evidence_limit: The army’s total of 640 sorties includes Breslau and other tasks. Fires seen by crews cannot establish casualties, the effect on German units, or how the raid affected the following day’s Soviet ground advance. No German unit is identified as the patrol contact.
source: Battle for Berlin, Soviet archive document edition
locator: Document 138, 18th Air Army operational summary no. 116, 26 April, pp. 187–190, f. 480, op. 7106, d. 231, ll. 62–65; separate document 143, 16th Air Army after-action report, pp. 201–203

case: Fighters over Gold, Juno and Sword
mission: Danny Browne recalled leading No. 441 Squadron RCAF on four beach patrols, starting at 06:25. The Canadian mission table records beach patrols for the squadron.

mission: Nos. 298 and 644 Squadrons each supplied three Halifax tugs for the six assault gliders. Their passengers included the 2nd Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry.

case: Which reinforcements can be traced to a French field?
mission: The 7 June transfer table identifies II./JG 3 bound for Évreux, III./JG 3 for Saint-André-de-l’Eure and IV.(Sturm)/JG 3 for Dreux. case: Why two different Gruppen have been labelled III./JG 4

case: Different airfields, different consequences in Brussels
mission: I./JG 26 and III./JG 54 were sent to Grimbergen. II. and III./JG 26 were sent to Evere. Some aircraft were lost or turned back before reaching either field.
observed_effect: A member of 127 Wing’s ground crew at Evere recalled preparing four new Spitfires for squadron markings before the attack. source: J. Rickard, Operation Bodenplatte
locator: JG 26 and III./JG 54, target allocations and respective outcomes.

case: Which bombers actually received the Berlin escort?

case: What did the October escort and diversion reports establish?
mission: The 353rd and 56th Fighter Groups escorted the two B-17 task forces. The 352nd rendezvoused with the 93rd and 392nd Bombardment Groups' B-24s. Weather broke up B-24 assembly and only 21 of the 29 dispatched flew the subsequent diversion toward the Frisian Islands.
observed_effect: 303rd crews reported P-47s turning back for fuel. The Werneck school diary independently records German fighters and flak during the approach from the west. Schweinfurt's local raid history lists hits on the bearing works, a malt factory and Oberndorf.
evidence_limit: The headquarters account says the planned withdrawal escort could not take off. The B-24 diversion belongs outside the main B-17 count. The German observers do not identify which American group they saw.
source: Headquarters, VIII Bomber Command, Narrative of Operations, 14 October 1943
locator: 115th operation, printed pp. 4–5 (scan pp. 13–14), Fighter Escort and Mission No. 3 – Diversion

case: Why are there two German defensive effort totals?

observed_effect: The I. Jagdkorps diary recorded 567 aircraft committed. The wider Luftwaffenbefehlshaber Mitte return gave 833 and included the 7. Jagddivision. Schmid lists another 49 from Luftflotte 3.
evidence_limit: Command boundaries differ and neither series provides a unique-aircraft roster over Schweinfurt. Divisional participation cannot attribute American losses to a Geschwader or Gruppe.
source: Josef Schmid, German Air Defense in World War II, vol. I
source_type: USAF historical study by a former German commander using German wartime returns
locator: Section 11, pp. 50–52, 14 October 1943, I. Jagdkorps war diary and Luftwaffenbefehlshaber Mitte Ic return of 15 October

case: How much of the bearing industry was destroyed?
mission: The 303rd Bombardment Group again flew against Schweinfurt. The command used reconnaissance photographs to estimate that the raid had destroyed 75 percent of local bearing production capacity.
observed_effect: The RAF history's subsequent comparison with German records gives about 20 percent of finished stocks and 3.5 percent of machinery damaged in the October operation. These figures measure different things from the wartime estimate.
evidence_limit: The estimates do not identify damage attributable to the 303rd. A factory's damaged machinery, stock on hand, later output and national war production must each be measured separately.
source: Headquarters, VIII Bomber Command, Narrative of Operations, 14 October 1943
locator: Operation 115, Missions 1–3, diversionary B-24 force, weather and preliminary assessment

case: What did the Canadian night force contribute at Leipzig?
mission: No. 6 Group supplied 31 Lancasters from two squadrons and 98 Halifaxes from ten squadrons to the opening night raid. No. 419 Squadron's Form 541 records its own crews' work.
observed_effect: The group reconstruction identifies eighteen crews that failed to return, totalling 128 missing crew members. The original 419 diary allows individual sorties to be checked inside this national group.
evidence_limit: The missing count describes the first reporting outcome. The Canadian group's 129 aircraft exclude other Bomber Command groups. This night operation preceded the Eighth Air Force's daylight attack.
source: Richard Koval, 6 Group Bomber Command
source_type: group history compiled from operations records
locator: 19/20 February 1944, Leipzig, Canadian squadron list, aircraft and crews missing

case: Which German divisions met the daylight offensive?
mission: The German account places 1. and 2. Jagddivision against the northern force and 2. and 3. Jagddivision against the main force. The 2. Jagddivision appears in both contexts.
observed_effect: The German account separates 362 fighters employed from 155 that actually entered combat. A commitment total would overstate the number reported to have fought.
evidence_limit: Wood's wider German unit table also lists Gruppen from the fourth, fifth and seventh divisions and Ostmark. Its entries measure claims and losses by unit. They cannot supply a divisional split of the 155 aircraft reported in combat by the corps.
source: Josef Schmid, German Air Defense in World War II, vol. II
source_type: USAF historical study by a former German commander using German wartime returns
locator: Printed pp. 105–107 and 115–117, 20 and 24 February battle accounts and German command returns

case: Can the German claimant for one missing American escort be identified?
mission: John Mattie of the 353rd Fighter Squadron, 354th Fighter Group, lost P-51 43-12161 during the escort operation and became a prisoner. Missing Air Crew Report 2329 and his diary survive.
observed_effect: Heinz Bär of 6./JG 1 received official German credit for a P-51 in the area. A comparison of the two pilots' records favours Bär, with another claim by Hans-Heinrich König of 3./JG 11 still unresolved.
evidence_limit: The records establish Mattie's fate and Bär's claim independently. The authors identify the connection as probable. The claim record lacks a matching American serial.
source: John D. Mattie, wartime diary and Missing Air Crew Report 2329
source_type: wartime US airman diary and missing crew report reproduced together
locator: Diary pp. 25–83 and appendix C, report 2329, pp. 86–90

case: Steyr and Fiume had different bomber and escort histories
mission: The 2nd, 97th and 301st Bombardment Groups struck Steyr with 87 B-17s. Weather separated the 99th, whose 27 attacked Fiume. The 5th Wing reported that attacks on the Steyr bombers continued until the four withdrawal fighter groups appeared south of the target.
observed_effect: The wing recorded 16 B-17s lost in the Steyr operation, ten from the 2nd Group. The municipal account for Steyr records 212 dead, 371 injured and over 1,000 homeless. It describes the destruction of Building M, light damage to the engine factory and an intact heat-treatment section.
evidence_limit: The Steyr account cannot attribute individual impacts to a bomber group. The German I. Jagdkorps figure of 336 on 24 February covers its own reporting area and includes repeat sorties. It cannot establish the fighter force over Steyr.
source: 5th Bombardment Wing, February 1944 operations
locator: 24 February, Steyr and alternate Fiume, group assignments, bombing times and losses

case: What could reconnaissance establish about Gotha?
mission: The 392nd and 445th Bombardment Groups flew B-24s against the Gotha aircraft works. Hal Turell of the 445th's 703rd Squadron recalled that thirteen of the group's 25 aircraft failed to return.
observed_effect: The post-strike reconnaissance photograph shows damage to the works. The 392nd briefing's estimate of potential enemy aircraft production forgone was an expectation contingent on the duration of disruption.
evidence_limit: Structural damage and American group losses are observable in different records. They cannot establish a definite number of aircraft the factory failed to deliver or which defending formation shot down each bomber.
source: Hal Turell, 703rd Bombardment Squadron, on the Gotha mission
source_type: participant recollection published by the 445th Bomb Group
locator: 24 February 1944 account, editorial introduction and passage after bomb release
